articles.title: Pacific Fusion’s next fusion machine could clear a key hurdle to commercial power | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Pacific Fusion is one step closer to commercializing fusion power after breaking ground Tuesday on a facility in New Mexico designed to generate as much energy as it consumes.
“It’s a huge step forward for commercial fusion power,” Carrie von Muench, co-founder and chief operating officer at Pacific Fusion, told TechCrunch. “To our knowledge, there’s no such facility being constructed in the country.”
While fusion power startups have been making rapid progress, no experiment or device has been able to generate enough power to offset the energy used by the facility, a milestone the industry calls net facility gain. One device, at the National Ignition Facility, has shown that controlled fusion reactions can generate more energy than they consume, but it is still far short of what would be needed to power the facility.
Pacific Fusion aims to hit net facility gain by 2030, with an eye toward operating a commercial power plant in the mid-2030s. Its commercial-scale reactor will need to generate about five times more energy than the demonstration system, in part to power the additional equipment a power plant requires.
The new facility, in Albuquerque, will test Pacific Fusion’s approach to fusion, which uses intense, tightly coordinated pulses of electricity to create a magnetic field around a fuel target about the size of a pencil eraser, squeezing it until the fuel atoms fuse.
The demonstration facility will be able to fire a handful of “shots” per day, Keith LeChien, co-founder and chief technical officer at Pacific Fusion, told TechCrunch. A full-size power plant will need to complete one shot per second.
The pulses of electricity will be generated by 156 pulser modules, each of which contains 32 circular stages made up of 10 bricks. Each brick consists of two capacitors, which store power, and one switch, which releases it. Earlier this year, Pacific Fusion tested a one-third-scale version of a pulser module, which released 440 gigawatts of peak power in 80 nanoseconds. The results were good enough to greenlight the demonstration facility.
In addition to demonstrating net facility gain, Pacific Fusion’s new campus will also host national security-related experiments involving high-yield fusion. The U.S. government has other sites that conduct similar research, like the National Ignition Facility, though that facility is starting to show its age. Each pulse of the new demonstration system will generate on the order of 100 megajoules, about 10 times the output of the National Ignition Facility, LeChien said.
“This exists nowhere in the world,” he said. “China is building these types of facilities, and we intend to be the first to deliver them.”
Pacific Fusion has moved swiftly in the last few years. The company was founded in 2023, making it one of the younger entrants to the field. It’s also among the best-funded fusion startups, having raised over $1 billion in a milestone-based Series A round.
The large, gated funding round allowed the company to plan further in advance, eliminating the need to fundraise every few years, von Muench said. “I don’t think it would have been possible to move at this speed if we hadn’t designed the capital stack the way that we have.”
Pacific Fusion will need every advantage it can get in the race to deliver a commercial power plant. The field is filling up with similarly well-funded startups, including Commonwealth Fusion Systems, Helion Energy, Proxima Fusion, and Inertia Enterprises, all of which are aiming to connect a fusion power plant to the grid by the mid-2030s, if not earlier.

articles.title: Intuit guides Mailchimp to zero growth and splits it out
articles.text:
Intuit is moving Mailchimp out of its main business and into a segment of its own. The first standalone forecast it has ever published for the marketing tool is for no growth at all.
Mailchimp will bring in $1,256mn to $1,266mn in fiscal 2027, Intuit said on Tuesday. That range runs from minus 1% to zero.
The company set out the change in its fourth quarter results. From 1 August 2026 it began running Mailchimp as a separate operating segment. It becomes a separate reportable segment in fiscal 2027, and Intuit points readers to its investor fact sheet for the detail.
The rest of the company grew 14%
Intuit took $21.4bn in revenue over the year to 31 July, up 14%. GAAP operating income rose 20% to $5.9bn.
Chairman and chief executive Sasan Goodarzi led on the milestone. “We surpassed $20 billion in revenue for the full year with growth fueled by our Big Bets which collectively grew 34 percent and represented 30 percent of full-year revenue,” he said.
Guidance for the coming year is softer. Intuit expects $23,279mn to $23,512mn, which is growth of 9% to 10%.
One number in the tables ran the other way. Fourth quarter GAAP earnings per share came in at $1.34, against $1.35 a year earlier, and GAAP net income fell to $363mn from $381mn.
The subhead advertises revenue growth of 14% in the quarter. It does not mention the earnings line.
Every growth figure comes with a Mailchimp exception
Read the segment lines and a pattern appears. Intuit quotes almost every number twice, once as reported and once without Mailchimp.
Global Business Solutions revenue rose 16% to $12.9bn. Excluding Mailchimp it rose 18%. Online Ecosystem revenue rose 19% to $9.9bn, or 23% excluding Mailchimp.
The widest gap is in Online Services, which grew 16% as reported and 24% without Mailchimp. That is eight percentage points of growth sitting in one product.
Intuit publishes no standalone Mailchimp revenue for fiscal 2026 anywhere in the release. The only hard number it gives is the one in next year’s forecast.
A $293mn charge the release never explains
Intuit booked $293mn of restructuring costs in the fourth quarter. It booked $15mn across the whole of the previous year.
The entire charge landed in one quarter. The first three quarters of fiscal 2026 each recorded nothing.
No paragraph of the release announces it. The figure appears in the financial tables, and then in a risk factor that refers to “our restructuring plan (Plan)” and warns that the estimate is preliminary and subject to change.
Intuit gives no headcount, no geography, no savings target and no description of what the plan involves. Goodarzi’s quote says the company is “making deliberate choices to create a stronger foundation for durable long-term growth”.
That silence is now standard. Zillow, which calls itself AI-native, cut 500 jobs without saying whether AI was the reason. Salesforce cut 133 more and did not mention AI in the filings either. Employers across the sector are also quietly rehiring the people AI replaced.
The Big Bets number rests on nothing
Goodarzi’s 34% claim is the spine of the release. It is also unsupported.
Intuit never names its Big Bets. It never lists them, never itemises them, and never reconciles the 34% to any line in the accounts. No table carries the figure and no footnote explains it.
30% of $21.4bn implies roughly $6.4bn of revenue. Intuit does not state that either.
The detail may arrive at its investor day on 17 September. Until then the headline number in the results has no working shown behind it.
TurboTax sold fewer returns and charged more
TurboTax revenue rose 7% to $5.3bn. Unit volumes fell.
TurboTax handled 39 million US federal returns, down from 39.9 million. Desktop units dropped 7%.
The growth came from price and mix. TurboTax Live revenue rose 37% and now accounts for 53% of all TurboTax revenue, a majority for the first time.
Credit Karma was the strongest named business, up 20% to $2.6bn on personal loans, car insurance and credit cards.
The goalposts move on 1 August
Intuit is also changing how it reports. From 1 August it stops excluding share-based compensation from its non-GAAP figures.
That matters for anyone comparing years. Share-based pay came to $2,056mn in fiscal 2026, and next year’s guidance absorbs $2,020mn of it, worth $5.81 a share.
So non-GAAP earnings per share guidance of $22.88 to $23.12 sits below the $24.27 Intuit reported this year, while the release still describes it as growth of 23% to 24% against a restated base.
The move itself is unusually shareholder-friendly. Most companies keep the add-back.
Where this lands in Europe
Mailchimp is one of the tools European small businesses reach for first, alongside Klaviyo and HubSpot, which reversed an AI feature after a customer revolt in July. A supplier guiding its own product to zero growth is a signal to anyone who has built a mailing list on it.
The competitive picture explains part of it. Salesforce paid $3.6bn for Fin, the Intercom-born support-AI firm, and generative tools now write the emails Mailchimp was bought to help send.
Intuit’s own international line grew 10% on a constant currency basis, against 14% for the group. Europe is not where its growth is.
What to watch next
The first thing is the September investor day, where the Big Bets should acquire definitions and numbers.
The second is the restructuring plan. Intuit has told investors the charge is preliminary, which means a further figure is coming, and a further figure will be harder to publish without explaining it.
The third is the first clean Mailchimp quarter. From fiscal 2027 the product reports on its own, and a business Intuit bought to sit at the centre of small-business marketing will have nowhere to hide its growth rate.
Intuit spent $5.5bn buying back its own shares this year, up 96%, and raised its dividend 15%. That is a company returning cash rather than finding places to put it.

articles.title: Sony phones in an update to the midrange Xperia 10 and slaps a sizable price hike on it - Engadget
articles.text:
Sony phones in an update to the midrange Xperia 10 and slaps a sizable price hike on it
The Xperia 10 VIII offers few upgrades for a lot more money.
It may no longer be selling its Xperia phones in the US, but Sony is still making them for other markets, and it has just launched the Xperia 10 VIII. Ostensibly an upgrade to last year's Xperia 10 VII, this is another firmly midrange Android phone with a remarkably similar spec sheet to its predecessor.
The Xperia 10 VIII sticks with a 6.1-inch 2340 x 1080 OLED display, with the only notable difference being that it can get 50 percent brighter than on the previous model. Also the same as before is the Snapdragon 6 Gen 3 processor paired with 8GB of RAM and 5,000mAh battery. 128GB of storage is the default offering.
The camera setup is also unchanged from the Xperia 10 VII, so once again you're shooting with a 50MP f/1.9 main camera, twinned with a 13MP ultrawide lens. There's seemingly no change to the 8MP front camera either.
Of course, Sony wouldn't dream of putting out a new phone that is exactly the same as the one it replaces for substantially more money, so rest assured that you're getting 15 percent louder speakers, and quick access to digital payment tools with a double tap of the power button. A feature like that might just catch on.
The Xperia 10 VIII has a "translucent" rear panel design and is available in three colors, which are Frozen White, Frosted Grey and Misty Lilac. If you want one, you can expect some very likely RAMpocalypse-influenced sticker shock. In the UK, the Xperia 10 VIII costs £549 (around $750), which is £150 ($205) more expensive than its markedly similar predecessor cost last year. If that doesn't put you off, and you're able to purchase one, the Xperia 10 VIII will be available in September.

articles.title: Trump is upping the price of Big Tech’s favorite visa
articles.text:
In the span of a few hours on Monday, the Department of Homeland Security announced that it would be implementing a fee of over $103,000 on H-1B visas, and news broke that the State Department plans on revoking the visas of up to 200,000 asylum seekers — which, according to The Associated Press, would be the largest mass visa revocation in US history.
Trump is upping the price of Big Tech’s favorite visa
Want to hire a foreign worker? Give Trump a $130,000 check.
More than a year into President Donald Trump’s second term, it’s become clear that the only way Trump can get the deportation numbers he wants is by stripping legal immigrants of status. Beyond having ICE arrest, detain, and deport immigrants, the administration is pressuring noncitizens to “self-deport,” in some cases imposing civil fines on them and threatening to seize their assets. It’s creating legal hurdles not only for new legal immigrants but for those already in the country, and in the process, likely hurting businesses and social services nationwide.
H-1B visas are often seen as synonymous with Big Tech, in no small part because Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft are the three biggest employers of H-1B workers. A federal judge struck down Trump’s previous attempt to raise the cost of these high-skilled employment visas in June, but not until over 70 employers paid the $100,000 fee. Now Trump wants to raise the cost to $103,265. Advocates and business leaders are worried Trump will soon come after the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program, which DHS hinted may soon carry a $100,000 fee of its own. OPT lets international students work in their field of study for 12 months, with extensions of up to 24 months for some STEM students and additional extensions for holders of certain graduate degrees.
“Every single other pathway is harder, outlawed, eliminated, more bureaucratic, more difficult across the board.”
“This is clearly unlawful,” said Todd Schulte, the president of FWD.us, an immigration reform organization founded by Mark Zuckerberg and other tech executives in 2013. “We don’t have to guess what this is for. This is to get rid of the OPT and H-1B program, which will have upstream and downstream devastating consequences: companies will be started elsewhere, people will be hired elsewhere.”
This won’t just hurt the tech industry. The previous fee hike exacerbated labor shortages at rural hospitals across the country and Alaska public schools, both of which have increasingly turned to high-skilled immigrant workers in the wake of local population decline. If the $100,000 fee was an inconvenience for Amazon and Meta, it was utterly catastrophic for rural communities already having trouble attracting qualified candidates.
Foreign workers aren’t the only legal immigrants Trump is targeting. According to the AP, which broke the news, the State Department will rescind up to 200,000 business and travel visas issued between 2016 and 2026 to people who applied for asylum after arriving in the US. Beyond limiting their ability to travel outside the country, this move won’t change much for asylum seekers who came to the US on nonimmigrant visas — at least not for now. But Schulte said the visa revocations are part of Trump’s efforts to gut the humanitarian immigration system. “Every single other pathway is harder, outlawed, eliminated, more bureaucratic, more difficult across the board,” he said. “It’s an all-of-government approach.”
The administration is framing this change as a way of closing a loophole in the asylum system: people coming to the country on nonimmigrant visas, ostensibly for work or pleasure, only to ask for asylum upon setting foot in the country.
“We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told the AP.
But the people who applied for asylum this way didn’t break any laws. In fact, a person needs to be present on US soil to apply for asylum; there’s no way to apply from outside the country. And Trump has closed most other avenues for humanitarian migration. There’s an effective “asylum ban” in place at the US-Mexico border. Refugee admissions have dropped to record lows, and the administration is now prioritizing the resettlement of white South Africans and denying almost everyone else.
In his second term, Trump has shown that the only immigrants he wants are those who look a certain way — or who can pay a small fortune for the privilege of working in America.

articles.title: This Projector Is a Hole-in-One as a Golf Simulator, but Subpar for Anything Else
articles.text:
This Optoma laser projector is great for setting up a golf simulator in your living room, but mediocre video quality makes it less appealing for home entertainment.
Great for golf simulation. Continuous operation. Light and portable. Affordable. Easy to configure using the remote.
TIRED
No built-in smart TV OS. Outdated HDMI ports. Passable performance for home entertainment and gaming. Confusing remote for everything but the initial setup.
Indoor golf simulators aren't easy to set up, and they aren't inexpensive. It starts with a home cinema projector, but you also need a wide, open space for swinging clubs, a backdrop with netting, and a gaming laptop or desktop to run the software. I was on a mission to see if I could do this much more cheaply with an affordable projector.
I accomplished my goal successfully by building around the Optoma GT2400HDR short-throw projector. I skipped the most expensive components, like the backdrop and the clubs. Instead, I used a gaming laptop and controller I already owned, and played EA Sports PGA Tour, which is included with my PC Game Pass Ultimate account. While the projector isn’t a bad option for playing golf at home on the cheap, it’s not ideal for watching movies and TV shows. It also struggles with high-octane games, and it doesn’t even include a smart TV platform.
Made for Indoor Driving Ranges
Optoma describes the GT2400HDR as a laser-based short-throw projector designed for gaming, entertainment, and golf simulation (the latter being my main intention). It can project a screen size from 30 to 300 inches at Full HD 1080p (1920 x 1080) resolution. My goal in creating an indoor driving range was to keep costs as low as possible, so I planned to use my Xbox controller with a gaming laptop and play on a 100-inch screen while still feeling like I was out on the links. For a golf game, you can get by with a midrange computer or even use a golf sim app on your iPad. (To do that, you’ll need to cast to a device that supports AirPlay or connect through HDMI via an adapter.)
Photograph: John Brandon
For less than $1,300, the GT2400HDR is a reasonable option, especially since it works well as a basic golf sim and costs far less than 4K models that can run $5,000 or more. The GT2400HDR also has some interesting perks that make it ideal for long golfing sessions.
For starters, it’s rated for 24/7 continuous operation. That’s because the laser light source doesn’t need to cool down after a few hours and can last 30,000 hours total. (Optoma does recommend powering the unit off when not in use, though.) The laser light source does not use a bulb, so there is nothing to replace. Heat dissipation is amazingly good, as the projector tends to run cool, unlike some high-end models. The GT2400HDR has an IP6X dust rating, so it’s sealed better than some massive home theater projectors that cost $4,000—ironic, considering that if you’re spending that much, you would expect better dust protection.
The projector's light weight (just under 7 pounds) and portability make it a good match for golf simulation. I found it easy to position the projector on the floor and then use it on a table or even in another room without lugging it around like a massive brick.
I first had to figure out where to place it for the golf sim, though. As a short-throw projector, it should normally sit about 4 feet away from the screen. Since I wouldn’t be using actual golf clubs, I could set it on the floor in my windowless testing room; otherwise, I would have to mount it on the ceiling, away from swinging clubs. The projected image looked big enough that, when I started playing EA Sports PGA Tour, the players looked about as tall as they are in real life.
Photograph: John Brandon
I noticed Optoma offers an app to help with initial setup, but it’s a hassle to use. You have to install the app and sync over Bluetooth, but I found it was easier to just do the keystone adjustment with the included remote. (Also, Optoma did not include the required Bluetooth dongle even though it is normally part of the package.)
Fortunately, keystoning was easy with the remote because, during setup, you can just position the four corners of the image. I ran one HDMI cable for my laptop and one for an AV receiver for surround sound (I used a Yamaha RX300A). In less than 30 minutes, I had the projector running, and I was swinging with the pros at Augusta.
I will say, I had an absolute blast with the setup. I loved the massive screen for golf, and I was pleased I didn’t have to bother with golf clubs, a backdrop screen, netting, or anything else to replicate the experience. If you want to use real clubs and balls, there are quite a few golf sim apps like SkyTrak for both PC and tablets that scan your motion and render a virtual player, although the total cost can add up quickly, including the backdrop and other gear.
Even though I was using a controller to play a video game, I still felt like I was on the links because of the massive size, bright 4,200-lumen rating, and colorful picture.
Photograph: John Brandon
The GT2400HDR only runs at 1080p resolution, but it does so at low latency (only 8.4 milliseconds at 120 Hz). I wasn’t expecting home cinema quality at this price, and golf simulations don’t require subtle color variations like a theatrical movie, which might have scenes that take place at night. You need accurate greens and blues, and the GT2400HDR handled that well.
There are two HDMI ports, which is fairly common, but the projector does not support the latest HDMI 2.1 standard for eARC passthrough audio. That means no Dolby Vision, and if you connect an AV receiver, you could run into compatibility issues. For example, I tried using my Onkyo receiver and had some minor audio glitches.
The projector also doesn’t support Wi-Fi unless you add a streaming device like a Google TV or an Amazon Fire TV. It has a legacy VGA port if your device is still in the dark ages (e.g., an extremely old computer, but in reality it is still widely used for signage, in schools, and as a fail-safe port), both a 3.5-mm input and output, and (in another unusual twist) a 3D Sync port for connecting 3D glasses (which I didn’t test).
Photograph: John Brandon
The remote has one of the most confusing layouts of any projector I have used. It seems like it was designed for a bygone A/V era. There are way too many buttons, and they're very small. There are so many buttons that it all seemed like overkill, especially since you may only use those buttons occasionally. Indeed, once everything is running, I didn’t find the need to use the remote that often.
Performance off Course
Outside of golf simulation, the GT2400HDR was just average in just about every other way. I ran a few typical benchmarks, and the skin tone tests all looked bland and grayed out, as though every face looked the same. There just wasn’t enough dynamic tonal range. In a demo video, mist over a mountain scene blended into the white background and did not look distinct. In a scene involving a fence with green grass in the background—one of the best ways to test color quality—the GT2400HDR made everything look way too brown.
For movies, I watched a scene in The Batman with flares that look shockingly red on higher-end projectors like the Xgimi Titan Noir Max. Here, the reds were too dark, lacked shadow detail, and blended too much into the dark background. In a scene from the 4K Ultra Blu-ray version of Blade Runner 2049, where the main character arrives at a protein farm, several buildings should have rendered in distinct yellows and blues. Instead, the scene looked too grayed out, like a thin veneer covered the entire screen. Of course, it didn’t help that the 4K movie had to be downgraded to 1080p resolution.
Photograph: John Brandon
I won’t harp on these detriments too much, because the GT2400HDR is not meant to compete with a movie theater. I switched to a few more games and found that Red Dead Redemption 2 on an Xbox Series X looked pretty good, if a little too atmospheric. That’s a kind way of saying the contrast is not great. At times, it seemed like the projected image had more in common with an LCD computer monitor than a home cinema projector.
The GT2400HDR disappointed in its handling of what should be impressive updated graphics in Halo: Campaign Evolved. Instead of rich, vibrant-looking trees, they looked too bland, with flat, dull greens. In Assassin’s Creed: Black Flag Resynced, the colors in a level that takes place in Havana should pop when you walk through the town, but the blue tunics, yellow fruit, and green trees lacked vibrancy.
A news broadcast looked dull and bland, as did a World Cup match I rewatched. There’s a theme here: bland and dull colors. However, I was surprised that a dark scene of a character riding a bike in the movie Awake didn’t look terrible. I could make out faces and some colors, which is saying a lot since this scene is hard to render. An entire moonlit scene in House of the Dragon, via the HBO app on a Google TV Streamer, looked completely washed out until I switched to the Vivid picture mode, which helped a bit. It was all par for the course, no pun intended.
I then watched scenes from Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 and noticed that Cinema picture mode did help punch up the colors a bit. Super Mario Galaxy lacked the color vibrancy and clarity that it normally has and looked like it was playing on a cheap computer monitor (e.g., poor contrast and less-than-vivid colors). When I switched to The Ark on YouTube TV, the colors looked much better because the show features bright, well-lit interior shots in almost every scene.
In the end, everything I tested and benchmarked on the GT2400HDR looked just OK, but I liked how well this projector works as a golf simulator. It can run all day long for multiple rounds, has low latency to make sure your controller nudges translate to accurate drives, and looks massive and bright on a large projector screen in a dark room. Sure, just about everything else is average, but if you are into golf, this is a good low-cost entry-level option.

articles.title: Sự thật trần trụi khi "YouTube của Trung Quốc" xuất ngoại: Nước cờ bắt buộc của một đế chế đã cạn dưỡng khí ở sân nhà
articles.text:
Cuộc mở rộng ra toàn cầu của Bilibili không phải câu chuyện tham vọng, mà là câu chuyện của một nền tảng hết chỗ để lớn ở nhà.
Bilibili vừa phát hành phiên bản quốc tế của ứng dụng ra toàn cầu. Bản Android đã có mặt trên Google Play, còn bản iOS được Creator Hub của công ty cho biết sẽ đến sau, cùng với việc mở rộng thêm nhiều quốc gia, với nội dung phân phối toàn cầu, bản địa hóa tốt hơn và quy trình đăng ký không cần xác minh danh tính. Tính đến ngày 21/8, theo ghi nhận của Notebookcheck, ứng dụng đã vượt 5 triệu lượt tải trên Google Play.
Thay đổi thực chất nằm ở khâu đăng ký. Theo Semafor, phiên bản mới không còn đòi hộ chiếu hay giấy tờ tùy thân, thứ vốn bắt buộc với người dùng nước ngoài trên nền tảng chính bằng tiếng Trung suốt nhiều năm. Bilibili chưa bao giờ bị chặn bên ngoài Trung Quốc. Thứ giữ lượng người dùng quốc tế ở mức khiêm tốn không phải là tường lửa mà là thủ tục, và thủ tục đó vừa được gỡ.
Động cơ thật nằm trong báo cáo tài chính, không nằm trong thông cáo
Quý I/2026, tổng doanh thu Bilibili đạt 7,47 tỷ nhân dân tệ, khoảng 1,08 tỷ USD, chỉ tăng 7% so với cùng kỳ. Bóc tách ra thì bức tranh sắc nét hơn nhiều: quảng cáo tăng 30% lên 2,59 tỷ nhân dân tệ và chiếm 35% tổng doanh thu, dịch vụ giá trị gia tăng chỉ tăng 4%, còn mảng game giảm 12% xuống 1,52 tỷ nhân dân tệ. Nói cách khác, công ty hiện chỉ còn đúng một động cơ tăng trưởng. Và để thấy tốc độ giảm nhanh đến mức nào, chỉ cần so với ba quý trước đó: quý II/2025, doanh thu còn tăng 20%, mảng game tăng tới 60%. Từ 20% xuống 7% trong ba quý không phải một cú vấp, đó là một trần.
Phần còn lại của bảng cân đối cũng không cho phép thong thả. Bilibili kết thúc quý I với 24,19 tỷ nhân dân tệ tiền mặt và đầu tư ngắn hạn, lợi nhuận ròng 202 triệu nhân dân tệ, đảo chiều từ mức lỗ cùng kỳ, lợi nhuận ròng điều chỉnh tăng 62% lên 585,4 triệu nhân dân tệ. Có tiền để tiêu, nhưng cũng có việc phải lo: theo phân tích của Panabee, ban lãnh đạo đang đối mặt với khoảng 2,49 tỷ USD trái phiếu chuyển đổi trong khi vốn hóa công ty ở mức 7,2 tỷ USD, và báo cáo quý II ngày 27/8 được xem là thời điểm nhà đầu tư đòi bằng chứng định lượng về khả năng sinh lời bền vững. Đặt cạnh nhau, việc tung app quốc tế đúng tám ngày trước kỳ báo cáo là một lựa chọn có tính toán.
Bối cảnh này cũng giải thích một chi tiết mà phần lớn bản tin bỏ qua: Bilibili từng có app quốc tế và tự tay khai tử nó. Tháng 7/2025, công ty thông báo gỡ bản quốc tế biểu tượng trắng khỏi các kho ứng dụng từ ngày 5/8, với lý do app chính đã hỗ trợ đầy đủ tính năng. Truyền thông Trung Quốc khi đó dẫn nguồn cho biết động thái nhằm tối ưu ma trận sản phẩm, tránh phân tán nguồn lực và tập trung cho app chính; bản iOS quốc tế thực tế đã ngừng cập nhật từ 3/4/2025. Mười ba tháng sau, bản quốc tế trở lại với logic ngược hẳn: năm ngoái là gộp về trong nước để tiết kiệm nguồn lực, năm nay là mở feed chung và đi tuyển người ở sáu thành phố. Thứ thay đổi giữa hai thời điểm không phải công nghệ, mà là tốc độ tăng trưởng trong nước.
Họ không đi tìm người xem, họ đi tìm người làm nội dung
Đây là điểm phân biệt lần mở rộng này với mọi lần trước. Trong tài liệu chia sẻ ở kênh Discord dành cho creator, công ty tự giới thiệu là nơi các influencer kiếm tiền và tiếp cận nhóm người dùng được mô tả là "Gen Z Coded, khá giả và học vấn cao", đồng thời cho biết một marketplace kết nối creator quốc tế với nhãn hàng cho nội dung tài trợ đang được phát triển. Song song, công ty tuyển community manager tại Los Angeles, London, Mexico City, São Paulo, Istanbul và Tokyo, cùng các vị trí xây dựng hệ thống kiểm duyệt nội dung bằng AI đặt tại Singapore.
Quy mô để chào mời thì không thiếu. Quý I/2026, lượng người dùng hoạt động hàng tháng vượt 376 triệu, người dùng hoạt động hàng ngày tăng 8% lên 115 triệu, tổng thời gian sử dụng tăng 19%. Thời gian xem trung bình đạt 119 phút mỗi ngày, con số mà phần lớn nền tảng phương Tây không chạm tới. Bilibili cũng đã mời được vài gương mặt phương Tây đăng video lên trang tiếng Trung, nổi bật nhất là MrBeast.
Nhưng có một câu hỏi mà bộ tài liệu marketing chưa trả lời, và nó là câu hỏi quan trọng nhất với bất kỳ creator nào đang cân nhắc: chia sẻ doanh thu ra sao. Lịch sử trong nước của Bilibili ở khoản này không đẹp. Chương trình Kích lệ Sáng tạo, nguồn thu nền tảng chính của UP chủ vừa và nhỏ, từng gây khủng hoảng niềm tin khi bị điều chỉnh thuật toán. Nhiều UP chủ phản ánh với báo chí Trung Quốc rằng sau khi đổi phiên bản, một video 10.000 lượt xem từ mức thu tối thiểu 16 tệ chỉ còn 2 đến 3 tệ, giảm hơn 80%, và thu nhập từ chương trình này không còn đủ để coi là nguồn sống. Truyền thông Đài Loan khi đó cũng ghi nhận khoản phân chia mà UP chủ nhận được trong đợt ngừng đăng bài tập thể chỉ bằng một phần ba đến một nửa so với năm 2022, và số video đăng tải trung bình mỗi tháng giảm từ khoảng 22,5 triệu ở quý I/2023 xuống 18,9 triệu ở quý II.
Một nền tảng từng để cộng đồng sáng tạo bản địa mất lòng tin về tiền, giờ đi mời cộng đồng sáng tạo quốc tế bằng lời hứa về tiền. Đó là khoảng cách mà không tin tuyển dụng nào lấp được, và nó sẽ quyết định lần mở rộng này thành hay bại.
Anime, kiểm duyệt và hàng rào mang tên châu Âu
Song song với cuộc đối đầu ồn ào với YouTube, Bilibili bước vào một trận địa khác lặng lẽ hơn nhưng dễ thắng hơn. Crunchyroll, nền tảng anime lớn nhất ngoài Nhật Bản thuộc sở hữu của Sony, vừa trải qua sáu tháng làm phật lòng người dùng. Gói miễn phí có quảng cáo bị khai tử ngày 31/12/2025, đồng nghĩa từ 1/1/2026 mọi nội dung đều cần thuê bao trả tiền. Chỉ một tháng sau, từ ngày 2/2/2026, toàn bộ các gói tại Mỹ tăng giá: Fan từ 7,99 lên 9,99 USD, Mega Fan từ 11,99 lên 13,99 USD, Ultimate Fan từ 15,99 lên 17,99 USD.
Bilibili bước vào đúng khoảng trống đó với mô hình khác hẳn: một lượng lớn nội dung miễn phí, thư viện lai giữa YouTube và nền tảng anime, cùng mức giá cắt sâu dưới đối thủ. Với người xem donghua, tức hoạt hình Trung Quốc, lợi thế còn rõ hơn vì phần lớn tác phẩm do chính Bilibili sản xuất.
Vấn đề là bản quyền anime Nhật vốn được cấp theo lãnh thổ, và Bilibili nắm quyền ở châu Á chứ không phải toàn cầu. Một app phân phối toàn cầu chồng lên một thư viện giới hạn địa lý là bài toán pháp lý phải giải trước khi nó thành tranh chấp. Chuyện bản quyền đã được nêu ngay tuần đầu: khi các creator trên X nhắc lại tình trạng video bị đăng lại trái phép, tài khoản Creator Hub trả lời rằng đội ngũ sẽ xử lý nội bộ và tiếp nhận nghiêm túc các báo cáo vi phạm trong quá trình mở rộng toàn cầu.
Rủi ro lớn hơn nằm ở một câu tưởng như vô hại. Tài khoản marketing của Bilibili khẳng định nội dung trên trang Mỹ và trang Trung Quốc sẽ như nhau. Với creator, đó là lời mời hấp dẫn vì đồng nghĩa tiếp cận thẳng 376 triệu người dùng thay vì bị nhốt trong một phiên bản quốc tế èo uột. Nhưng nếu hai kho nội dung là một, thì tiêu chuẩn kiểm duyệt nào sẽ được áp dụng, và áp lên ai. Ở Mỹ, câu hỏi quen thuộc là liệu Bilibili có nhận kết cục như TikTok.
Ở châu Âu, cơ chế khác và không cần đến lệnh cấm. Theo phân tích của The Next Web, Đạo luật Dịch vụ Kỹ thuật số áp dụng ngay khi một nền tảng phục vụ người dùng EU, và ở ngưỡng 45 triệu người dùng hàng tháng, nền tảng bị xếp nhóm rất lớn kèm nghĩa vụ kiểm toán, đánh giá rủi ro và mở dữ liệu cho giới nghiên cứu. Brussels đã dùng đúng bộ công cụ này với doanh nghiệp Trung Quốc khi phạt Temu 200 triệu euro vì sản phẩm không an toàn. Trớ trêu là chính quyết định bỏ xác minh danh tính, nước cờ tăng trưởng mạnh nhất, lại là điểm đáng theo dõi nhất, bởi DSA buộc nền tảng phải đánh giá rủi ro do chính thiết kế của mình tạo ra, trong đó có rủi ro với trẻ vị thành niên.
Thứ Bilibili mang ra thế giới không phải công nghệ.
YouTube không thiếu hạ tầng, Crunchyroll không thiếu bản quyền.
Thứ Bilibili có là một cấu trúc cộng đồng mất hơn một thập kỷ mới xây được, với văn hóa bình luận đạn trôi ngang màn hình mà chưa nền tảng phương Tây nào sao chép thành công, và họ bước vào đúng lúc YouTube đang phòng thủ nhiều phía, khi Netflix đẩy mạnh podcast video và nội dung hướng creator, còn Google được cho là đang đàm phán trả tiền cho các kênh để đăng độc quyền trước thay vì phát đồng thời mọi nơi. Thứ Bilibili thiếu là lòng tin: Thiếu ở phía creator, thiếu ở phía cơ quan quản lý châu Âu, và thiếu ở phía chính những người dùng cũ từng bị lấy mất app quốc tế một lần rồi.
Với thị trường Việt Nam, rào cản gần như không còn, vì bản toàn cầu vốn đã hỗ trợ tiếng Việt bên cạnh tiếng Anh, Indonesia, Thái, Mã Lai và Ả Rập, phần vướng còn lại là thủ tục đăng ký thì vừa được gỡ.
Câu hỏi thú vị hơn dành cho người làm nội dung: Một nền tảng 376 triệu người dùng đang chủ động đi mời, giữa lúc kiếm tiền trên các nền tảng cũ ngày càng chật, là lời mời khó từ chối. Nhưng lời mời nào cũng có điều khoản, và điều khoản là thứ Bilibili chưa công bố.

articles.title: Gamma acquires Accel-backed design startup Lica | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Presentation startup Gamma has acquired Accel-backed design startup Lica in a bid to build out its own design research lab, TechCrunch has learned exclusively. Lica’s co-founders will lead the effort.
Lica started off as an app that could turn screenshots and recordings into project presentations and videos. Founded by Priyaa Kalyanaraman and Purvanshi Mehta in 2023, the company a year later raised $4 million from investors including Accel, South Park Commons, and Village Global. Over the past couple of years, it has focused on working with e-commerce sites to create marketing videos that adhere to brand guidelines.
Kalyanaraman said Lica wanted to build AI models around communication methods, including video and design, and the founders were familiar with Gamma’s CEO, Grant Lee, as both companies are backed by Accel and South Park Commons. Those conversations eventually led to the acquisition.
“We have a very similar North Star vision of wanting to make visual communication easy. We focused a lot on frontier research and making sure that became accessible to users. But that’s just one part of the solution. Gamma had focused a lot on building distribution, taking the application to 100 million-plus users. Given how fast things are moving, we decided to join forces,” Kalyanaraman told TechCrunch.
Gamma will continue to focus on helping people build presentations, but like other design companies, it’s also started offering image generation. The company says it now wants to explore different formats of communication with the new research division.
“Presentations for us are today a core use case, but how do we expand what presentations look and feel like, and how do people engage with them in the future? What visuals are possible? How interactive are they? These [questions] all require us to think deeply about the core responsibility of communication. This is why we’re excited to invest in this area, because we don’t think anybody else is thinking at that level,” Lee said.
Lica’s Mehta said the new research division would work on customizing the presentation and communication styles of AI models for different audiences and tastes.
“The point of the presentation is to communicate a large goal. We are thinking about building a platform where these two goals can be personalized to such an extent that you just get a really good output, and then you’re able to edit for different audiences,” she said.
Gamma didn’t reveal what products it plans to build as a result of this acquisition, but it did say that it wants to create fluid, multimodal presentations and other communication modalities.
AI presentation startups have received tons of investor attention and money over the last few years. Prezent raised $50 million in two rounds; Gamma raised $68 million at a $2.1 billion valuation; and Presentations.ai was also backed by Accel. We’re even starting to see some consolidation in this category: Earlier this month, OpenAI acquired NextSlide.

articles.title: OpenAI's buildout chief is out as leasing comes back
articles.text:
OpenAI has confirmed that the executive running its data centre buildout has left, and it has already broken up the job he was doing.
Chris Malone, its head of data centers, is no longer with the company, an OpenAI spokesperson told Dina Bass at Bloomberg on Monday. Anissa Gardizy broke the story earlier that day for The Wall Street Journal.
Malone joined in March 2025, shortly after OpenAI announced Stargate. That is the programme it runs with Oracle and SoftBank to build the computing capacity its models need, and its flagship site is still going up in Abilene, Texas.
The job did not stay as one job
OpenAI has made leadership changes inside its infrastructure team and appointed a chief technology officer to lead computing capacity, the Journal reported.
The company is also reviving some data centre initiatives, specifically projects that would involve leasing entire facilities. Other people are leading that effort in Malone’s place.
That is the part worth reading twice. This is not a vacancy waiting to be filled. The brief has been split, and the piece of it that is growing fastest now sits with someone else.
Leasing is a different strategy from building
Stargate is a construction programme. Leasing whole facilities is a procurement one, and it moves the risk, the timetable and the counterparties.
Building means land, permits, grid connections and a decade of commitments. Leasing means taking capacity somebody else has already financed, faster and at a price.
A company that is reviving the leasing route while its head of construction leaves is telling you something about which route it now favours.
The run of departures started in April
Kevin Weil, the former product chief, left in April. Fidji Simo, who oversaw much of the core business, stepped down last month after taking medical leave.
Brad Lightcap, the chief operating officer, announced this month that he was leaving for a new project after eight years. The head of safety went in July, after the company folded safety back into research.
Two weeks ago OpenAI named its second chief revenue officer in under a year, hiring Dali Rajic, president and chief operating officer of the Alphabet-owned security firm Wiz. He succeeds Denise Dresser, the former Slack chief executive, who took the job only last December.
Counting Malone, that is seven senior names gone or replaced since April.
The frame is the listing
OpenAI’s chief financial officer Sarah Friar told staff last week that the company will go public in 2027, or sooner.
Companies remake their leadership before a listing, and some of this is that. A public company needs the executives Wall Street expects to see, and it needs them in post long enough to sign things.
The simpler reading also holds. People who survive a build of this intensity tend to leave once the equity vests, particularly when the next phase looks like procurement rather than construction.
What the job had become
Running data centres for an AI lab is no longer a property function. It is a power function, and OpenAI has said as much through its hiring.
The company advertised for a power trading lead in August. That makes electricity a position on its books rather than a line on a utility bill.
That is a different job from the one Malone took in March 2025. It changed underneath him inside 18 months.
The scale involved
OpenAI is planning a $30bn data centre in Georgia. It has also been pushing into Ohio, where Nvidia has discussed guaranteeing $250bn of financing for the buildings that will house its chips.
Oracle has said a single AI data centre could expose it to a $7bn power guarantee. SoftBank has raised a $60bn bond partly to keep the OpenAI bet funded.
Each of those is a different counterparty on different terms. Somebody has to hold all of them in one plan.
What is still not known
OpenAI confirmed the departure but gave no reason for it. No source names where Malone is going.
Bloomberg sent him a message on LinkedIn and he did not immediately respond. The company has not named the chief technology officer for computing capacity in either account.
Departures at this level rarely come with a stated reason, and the absence of one proves nothing either way.
Why this is not like the sales exits
A company can replace a revenue chief inside a quarter and the pipeline survives. OpenAI has now done it twice in a year.
A data centre programme runs on relationships with utilities, planning authorities, construction firms and grid operators. Those relationships sit with individuals, interconnection queues run for years, and so do the contracts.
It is also the function where a mistake costs most. A site that cannot get power on schedule strands capital the company has already committed.
Europe is running the same race differently
Everything named here is American. Stargate, Abilene, Georgia, Ohio.
OpenAI has built its compute programme almost entirely in the United States, where land is cheaper and permitting faster than in most of Europe.
Europe’s constraint is not executive turnover but connection. Operators here queue for grid capacity rather than compete for it, and the buildout has been drifting to markets where the queue is shorter.
The leasing pivot matters here too. European colocation operators sell exactly the product OpenAI is now reported to want, which is finished capacity somebody else has already connected.
What to watch next
The first signal is the name. OpenAI has appointed a chief technology officer for computing capacity and has not said who it is.
The second is whether any announced site slips. Abilene, Georgia and Ohio all carry public timelines, and those timelines are the only public measure of whether this mattered.
The third is the prospectus. A company heading for a listing in 2027 will have to describe its compute commitments in writing, to regulators, and name the risks attached to them.
Key-person risk is a standard disclosure. OpenAI is about to find out how many of its own it has to list.

articles.title: What's the difference between Thunderbolt 4 and 5? - Engadget
articles.text:
What's the difference between Thunderbolt 4 and 5?
Thunderbolt 5 offers extremely fast data transfer and lots of power, but most devices can't take advantage of it.
To the casual observer, the difference between Thunderbolt 4 and Thunderbolt 5 boils down to another USB-C in a market saturated with them. For creators, serious gamers and IT teams, however, Thunderbolt 5 is an impressive and timely upgrade. Both standards use USB-C connectors, and both carry data, video and power. Both work with docks, external storage, displays and other compatible accessories. But Thunderbolt 5 doubles Thunderbolt 4's bidirectional data transfer and is capable of allocating 120Gbps in one direction and 40Gbps in the other. Thunderbolt 5 also brings 240 watts of power delivery to the table.
That's a significant leap for folks running several 4K displays or multiple high-resolution displays, including certain 8K configurations. Thunderbolt 5 is also backwards compatible with Thunderbolt 4, 3 and USB4 devices. Sure, a connection only works at the speed of its slowest component, but Thunderbolt 5 isn't meant for the casual gamer, light video editing, or older PC and Mac rigs.
For most people, Thunderbolt 4 remains more than enough for now. It can handle routine backups, a fast external SSD, charging, Ethernet and a typical single- or dual-monitor desk setup. On the flip side, those who move enormous files on the regular, use advanced docking stations or want to extend their creative workflows will find much to love with Thunderbolt 5.
Speed and display support
The greatest benefit of Thunderbolt 5 speed is that it provides data-heavy setups with some breathing room. A compatible Thunderbolt 5 external SSD, dock or PCIe expansion device can take full advantage of the new standard's 80Gbps baseline bandwidth, compared to Thunderbolt 4's 40Gbps. That doesn't necessarily mean every file transfer time will be cut in half, however. After all, several internal and external components play a role in speed.
Thunderbolt 5's extra bandwidth also improves Thunderbolt display support. For example, Thunderbolt 4 is built to support one 8K display or two 4K displays at 60Hz. Thunderbolt 5 can support a more demanding setup, like multiple 4K displays at higher refresh rates or certain 8K configurations. Again, the result depends on several factors (display-compression support, monitors involved, operating system, etc.), so buyers should always check their specs beforehand.
Charging, cables and value
Thunderbolt 5 is also a significant step up on the charging front. Apple's Thunderbolt 5 Pro cable supports up to 240W of power delivery, while Apple's Thunderbolt 4 Pro cable maxes out at 100W. High-end gaming laptops will benefit from Thunderbolt 5's added charging headroom, but only if their USB-C ports are designed for it. USB PD 3.1 raises USB-C's ceiling to 240W, with 140W, 180W and 240W versions more commonly available. For instance, high-end laptops like Lenovo's Legion 9i Gen 10 and Razer Blade 18 top out at 140W and 100W respectively.
From a purely Apple standpoint, cable length is another interesting difference for prospective buyers. Apple's Thunderbolt 4 Pro cables come in 1.8 and 3.0 meters for $129 and $159, respectively. The Thunderbolt 5 is only 1 meter and costs $69. The cable length is important in terms of signal integrity, and both of Apple's Thunderbolt 4 lengths feature active circuitry to reduce interference, driving up the price. Thunderbolt 5 Pro is shorter, but passive. Apple does manufacture a one-meter, passive Thunderbolt 4, but only as a packaged accessory with the Apple Studio Display, or through other vendors.
Most buyers should still go with the Thunderbolt 4 if you're looking for a mainstream laptop, a single-monitor desktop setup or a dock for your everyday, standard peripherals. It's still a high-end connection standard and is compatible with a huge range of existing accessories. If you're rocking a very fast external drive or multiple high-res, high-refresh rate displays, Thunderbolt 5 is a more than sensible upgrade. Ultimately, it's less about the connector shape and more about your workflow and whether or not you can use the bandwidth.

articles.title: Bitcoin tăng phi mã: Thị trường tiền số “dựng sóng”, nhà đầu tư “sôi sục” nguyên tuần
articles.text:
Thị trường tiền mã hóa tuần qua chứng kiến biến động đầy bất ngờ khi giá Bitcoin (BTC) liên tục dựng cột tăng trưởng, áp sát mốc 79.000 USD.
Sự bứt phá đột ngột này không chỉ hâm nóng tâm lý nhà đầu tư cá nhân mà còn châm ngòi cho hàng loạt cuộc tranh cãi giữa các định chế tài chính và giới phân tích toàn cầu.
Thị trường bùng nổ, Bitcoin bứt phá mạnh mẽ sau nhiều tháng
Trước khi cú bứt phá xảy ra, thị trường tiền mã hóa đã trải qua chuỗi ngày chìm trong không khí ảm đạm. Bitcoin liên tục "đi ngang" trong dải hẹp 62.000 – 64.000 USD với khối lượng giao dịch sụt giảm xuống mức thấp nhất trong nhiều tháng. Chỉ số Tham vọng & Sợ hãi (Fear & Greed Index) rơi xuống vùng "Sợ hãi" (Fear). Nhiều nhà đầu tư cá nhân rơi vào trạng thái nản lòng, các bài đăng trên Facebook, Threads hay X chủ yếu mang sắc thái than thở về việc "đu đỉnh" và tính chuyện rời bỏ thị trường.
Theo dữ liệu giao dịch ghi nhận trong ngày 24/8, giá Bitcoin dao động quanh mức 77.500 – 78.300 USD. Dù trải qua nhịp điều chỉnh nhẹ sau khi chạm đỉnh ngắn hạn ở mốc 78.900 USD, đồng tiền số lớn nhất thế giới vẫn duy trì đà bùng nổ với mức tăng kỷ lục hơn 23% chỉ trong vòng một tuần.
Sự trỗi dậy của Bitcoin đã lan tỏa sắc xanh rực rỡ ra toàn bộ hệ sinh thái tài sản kỹ thuật số. Vốn hóa thị trường của Bitcoin chạm ngưỡng 1.550 tỷ USD, kéo tổng giá trị thị trường tiền số vượt mốc 2.630 tỷ USD, tăng 0,9%.
Đồng tiền mã hóa lớn thứ hai thế giới ETH tăng thêm 1,62% so với hôm qua khi đạt mốc 2.463 USD. Đáng chú ý, XRP vượt BNB về mặt vốn hóa khi đạt 94,03 tỉ USD, trong khi vốn hóa của BNB hiện đạt 93,5 tỉ USD. Ngoài ra, các token khác như Solana, Hyperliquid, Doge lần lượt tăng 1,51%, 3,43% và 1,43%. Riêng Tron đi ngược xu hướng chung khi giảm 0,09%, hiện còn 0,3 USD mỗi token.
Thống kê thị trường cho thấy nhịp tăng nóng bắt đầu từ ngày 18/8, đẩy giá bứt phá từ vùng tích lũy 62.000 - 64.000 USD đi thẳng lên các mốc cao hơn.
Nguyên nhân khiến Bitcoin trong những ngày qua tăng phi mã là gì?
Lý giải về nguyên nhân giúp giá Bitcoin nhảy vọt từ vùng 64.000 USD lên áp sát 79.000 USD chỉ trong thời gian ngắn, các tổ chức phân tích tài chính chỉ ra đây là sự kết hợp của 3 yếu tố nền tảng.
Theo báo cáo từ The Kobeissi Letter nhận định, việc nợ công Mỹ chạm các cột mốc lịch sử cùng cam kết mua lại trái phiếu từ Bộ Tài chính Mỹ đã làm suy giảm sức hút của lợi suất trái phiếu chính phủ. Khi các kênh trú ẩn an toàn truyền thống giảm tỷ suất sinh lời, dòng tiền đầu cơ ngay lập tức chảy mạnh sang các tài sản có nguồn cung hữu hạn như Vàng và Bitcoin.
Trong khi đó, các quỹ ETF Bitcoin giao ngay tại Mỹ ghi nhận đợt hút ròng đột biến với hơn 650 triệu USD chỉ trong vài phiên giao dịch. Lực mua thực tế từ các định chế tài chính này đã đóng vai trò là "bệ đỡ" vững chắc cho đà tăng thời gian vừa qua.
Nhịp tăng nhanh qua các ngưỡng cản tâm lý 70.000 USD và 73.000 USD đã buộc phe bán khống phải chấp nhận cắt lỗ. Hàng trăm triệu USD vị thế Short bị thanh lý bắt buộc, vô tình tạo ra lực mua đuổi đẩy giá BTC tăng dựng đứng.
Các chuyên gia tranh cãi gay gắt về đà tăng của Bitcoin
Sự bứt phá đột ngột của Bitcoin đang chia rẽ sâu sắc giới phân tích toàn cầu giữa hai luồng quan điểm, một bên tin vào chu kỳ bùng nổ mới, bên còn lại cảnh báo rủi ro bẫy giá.
Cụ thể, CoinDesk dẫn lời Mati Greenspan, nhà sáng lập Quantum Economics, cho rằng đợt tăng giá vừa qua là tín hiệu thường thấy của đáy thị trường. "Xu hướng này được đánh dấu bằng một đợt tăng giá đột ngột, một 'nến xanh khổng lồ' phá vỡ các ngưỡng kỹ thuật. Những người đặt lệnh giới hạn chờ BTC giảm xuống 40.000 USD đang xem xét lại chiến lược". Ông cũng khẳng định khả năng thị trường giảm sâu lúc này là rất thấp nhờ tâm lý FOMO tăng mạnh, cộng hưởng với các động thái hành lang pháp lý tích cực từ Nhà Trắng, Quốc hội Mỹ, SEC và CFTC trong việc định hình khung quản lý tài sản mã hóa.
Ở chiều ngược lại, Jason Fernandes, nhà phân tích thị trường và đồng sáng lập AdLunam, cảnh báo nhà đầu tư không nên quá phấn khích: "Mọi người phải đặc biệt thận trọng nếu xem đây là dấu chấm hết cho thị trường gấu. Nếu không có dòng vốn ETF giao ngay bền vững và lãi suất vĩ mô được nới lỏng, Bitcoin có thể mất đà tăng giá khi chạm ngưỡng kháng cự".
Đồng quan điểm, Adam Morgan McCarthy, nhà nghiên cứu hàng đầu tại LO:TECH (London), đưa ra so sánh với thị trường truyền thống, ông đánh giá: "Vàng tăng mạnh khi Bộ Tài chính Mỹ tăng gấp đôi hoạt động mua trái phiếu - đó mới là tín hiệu vĩ mô thực sự. Nếu nhà đầu tư tìm nơi phòng ngừa rủi ro lạm phát, vàng là lựa chọn an toàn còn Bitcoin thì không".
Đợt tăng giá lần này đang đưa thị trường tiền mã hóa vào giai đoạn nhạy cảm. Sự kết hợp giữa dòng vốn đòn bẩy kỷ lục và những xung đột về góc nhìn vĩ mô khiến xu hướng tiếp theo của Bitcoin trở thành bài toán hóc chuẩn bị chờ lời giải trong quý IV./
Thiên Minh

articles.title: At just $8, you owe it to yourself to grab Inscryption
articles.text:
If you watched the Gamescom 2026 announcements, you might have caught a trailer for the bizarre, frenetic Pony Island 2: Panda Circus, a game from Daniel Mullins. In case you haven’t heard of him, get a crash course with a fantastic discount on Inscryption. Humble is currently selling Steam versions of the secret-packed deckbuilder for $7.99, a sizable discount from its usual price of $20. It’s compatible with Windows, macOS, and Linux machines.
At just $8, you owe it to yourself to grab Inscryption
If the Pony Island 2 trailer sparked your curiosity, one of Mullins’ earlier mind-bending games is discounted.
The game starts out as a fairly straightforward deckbuilding roguelike game with a dark atmosphere. Stick with it, and it’ll evolve, defying genres, breaking the fourth wall, and leading you through a twisted story with plenty of surprises. Part of the fun is discovering those twists yourself, so I won’t say anything else. It’s one of my personal favorite games, and it’s best to go in knowing as little as possible. Thankfully, taking the leap isn’t expensive at all.

articles.title: Border Wall Construction Threatens 6,000 Years of History on Private Lands
articles.text:
Outrage has exploded over border infrastructure that recently began tearing up pristine desert landscapes in Big Bend National Park. But there’s a quieter battle taking place on private lands in Texas, where the US border wall is set to cut across some of North America's richest archaeological sites, digging up ancient indigenous artifacts and fracturing millennia-old rock art in its path.
The US Department of Homeland Security and Customs and Border Protection awarded billions of dollars in contracts this year toward the construction of a wall and other barriers in West Texas along a remote 500-plus-mile (800-plus-kilometer) riverfront expanse of the US-Mexico border that includes Big Bend National Park and other idyllic parklands.
Bipartisan backlash against border wall construction in the national park was swift, ultimately prompting DHS to scuttle plans for a 30-foot steel bollard wall, instead replacing it with miles of riverside vehicle barriers and 200-plus miles of road construction. Bulldozers began clearing along the Rio Grande corridor near Santa Elena Canyon on August 6.
Construction has since been paused in the park in response to lawsuits. But the agency is still planning to construct the wall, as well as a web of road construction, over mountains and across canyons outside the national park. That includes private property that ranchers and other landowners say have archeological sites worth protecting, too. And they’re concerned that construction of the wall will bifurcate their own land and damage archeological sites, many of which have yet to be fully studied.
Archeologist Bryon Schroeder has been digging on rancher Jeff Fort’s property for two years. Schroeder runs Sul Ross University’s Center for Big Bend Studies, a research program dedicated to studying the cultural, historical, and archeological legacy of the region. He removes 4 inches (10 centimeters) of sediment at a time, and his meticulous digs have uncovered pottery and melted adobe slick building material from as early as the year AD 800. He’s found turquoise, too, and marine shells, both signs of trade outside the region. Evidence shows the site is related to Paquimé, an UNESCO World Heritage site that’s 200 miles away in Mexico.
Schroeder’s dig site, Canta Recio, is directly in the path of the proposed wall. Some of it is set to be bulldozed over. If the wall is built, other parts of the site will also become effectively inaccessible.
Schroeder likens Canta Recio to how Egyptians set up shop along the Nile, surmising the site was settled four or five times between 800 and 1400 by groups who were likely drawn to fertile land afforded by routine floods. Of course, those floods also mean that groups were eventually forced to move on when the Rio Grande overtopped its banks, only for another group to eventually settle the area once the silt firmed up. A settlement, a flood, an exit, on repeat.
“There's some bigger, cooler sites up the river that are just insane,” Schroeder said. “They have so much pottery, they have Mesoamerican copper bells, they have turquoise. They have all sorts of crazy stuff.”
The paradox facing Schroeder and other archeologists: They can't fully measure what's at risk because many of the archeological sites exist on private ranches and have never been studied.
That means construction may erase history before anyone gets to record it. A Customs and Border Protection spokesperson told WIRED that the agency is conducting environmental and cultural reviews to minimize impacts and balance operational needs with responsible land stewardship.
But previous studies haven’t stopped historically important sites from being sentenced to destruction. A 30-foot bollard wall is set to go right through the Polvo site, in Redford, Texas, which is home to a prehistoric village complete with burial ground dating back to the 1300s. The same site also has evidence of a Spanish mission that was built in the 1600s. Eagle Nest Canyon in Langtry, one of the most significant and intensively studied archeological sites in all of Texas, is also slated to see some form of barrier erected through it. That site includes the southernmost bison jump site in the US, where Native Americans hunted the animals en masse by funneling them over a cliff.
Patrick Zuberbueler, a rancher 350 miles downriver in Comstock, Texas, population 268, spent his youth picnicking in the shadows of 6,000-year-old rock art, with some displays up to 50 feet tall and hundreds of feet wide, across his family’s property. The government took some of that land by eminent domain in the 1960s and 1970s, forming the Amistad Reservoir and Seminole Canyon State Park, but he and his family still hold onto thousands of acres.
As a child, Zuberbueler would catch minnows in a stream running through Painted Shelter, a limestone rock shelter on his family’s property. To him, it was “a place we’d go picnicking.” To archeologist and rock art expert Carolyn Boyd, it’s “one of the most important archeological sites in the region.”
Painted Shelter has three distinct styles of rock art, painted between 6,000 and 1,000 years ago. Rock artworks encode stories and cosmologies, and are “libraries of human knowledge,” says Boyd, a research professor at Texas State University in San Marcos who founded Shumla Archaeological Research and Education Center in 1998.
Painted Shelter is also right in the path of border construction.
“A vehicle barrier going in just immediately above it will destroy the stream, and it will potentially destroy the paintings themselves,” says Boyd, one of the nation’s leading scholars on rock art.
Vibration from construction could potentially cause the limestone to spall, or sheet off, she says, leaving the rocky canvas in tatters. She knows of 12 other rock art sites across the region that are also at risk from construction, while another 79 will become inaccessible.
The region around the Zuberbueler ranch, known as the Lower Pecos Canyonlands Archeological District, was designated as a National Historic Landmark on January 13, 2021, under the first Trump administration. Federal law dictates that agencies “to the maximum extent possible undertake such planning and actions as may be necessary to minimize harm” to National Historic Landmarks. But with the National Historic Preservation Act one of dozens of laws waived by the Department of Homeland Security in its pursuit of a border wall, those requirements to minimize harm are off the table.
For Zuberbueler, pushing back against the border barrier isn’t just about the archaeology his land holds. It’s about the legacy of his great-grandfather, who started working the land in 1898.
“The ranch continues to shrink and shrink and shrink, and you can't effectively ranch something that way,” Zuberbueler says. “They're hurting our livelihood as producers.”
Boyd, who has dedicated four decades to unearthing the history behind the region’s rock art, says she feels like she’s living a nightmare. “Maybe it’s wishful thinking,” she says, but she hopes she can get the government to understand the significance of the region’s archeology and revise its plans to rely on technology to patrol the area rather than physical infrastructure.
But time is seemingly running short to make that case. Several miles of steel bollards lay in piles at staging areas, and several temporary workforce housing “man camps” have cropped up on newly cleared land across the region. Locals say wall contractors have already bulldozed private property before they were legally allowed to, damaging irrigation systems and clearing vegetation. But some locals aren’t ready to give up. And there are signs of resistance to development on private lands elsewhere, including suits filed earlier this month by residents in San Ygnacio, which sits about 275 miles further south of the Big Bend region.
“It's almost unfathomable to even put it into context, the different ways that this can be detrimental to us,” Zuberbueler said about the border construction. “We're not going to go down without a fight.”

articles.title: Apple rescues Hide My Email feature from the privacy scrap heap | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Apple has reneged on a planned change to its Hide My Email feature that users said would have made the privacy tool less effective.
Hide My Email is a privacy feature for paying iCloud+ users that generates a unique and disposable email address to give websites instead of a person’s real email address and still have emails route to their regular inboxes. The benefit of the email-hiding feature is that privately generated email addresses cannot be distinguished from regular Apple users with an @icloud.com email address. However, the feature still allows Apple to tell law enforcement who is behind a masked email address.
Earlier this year, the company said it would move users to @private.icloud.com, which users said would make it easier for websites to reject these email addresses during sign-ups. On social media and Reddit threads, users criticized the change as defeating the purpose of the service altogether.
The company confirmed an update on Monday that Hide My Email addresses “will remain” on @icloud.com, after previously saying it would move users to @private.icloud.com.
Apple did not give a reason for changing its decision, but Daring Fireball’s John Gruber, who first reported the about-face, said that Apple employees had objected to the change all along.
Earlier this year, 404 Media reported that a bug in Hide My Email revealed people’s real email addresses. Apple fixed the bug more than a year after it was first made aware that emails rejected as spam would leak the masked users’ real email addresses.

articles.title: The Witcher 3 is getting a remaster
articles.text:
CD Projekt Red is remastering The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, the hit RPG that first launched in 2015, and the updated game will be available starting September 29th. The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered will bring improvements to visuals and combat, a “reimagined” skill tree, and more, and it also includes the first two expansions, Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine.
The Witcher 3 is getting a remaster
The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered launches in September.
Remastered will be a free upgrade for players who own the base game on GOG, Steam, Epic Games Store, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X / S. With the launch of Remastered, The Witcher 3 will also be coming to the Nintendo Switch 2.
This remastered version of The Witcher 3 (which follows a next-gen upgrade released in 2022) is the start of a big push for the franchise over the next few years. CDPR is set to launch a brand new Witcher 3 expansion, titled Songs of the Past, in 2027, and it’s aiming to release its next mainline Witcher game, The Witcher 4, in 2028.

articles.title: Two teens in a thousand used it. Meta kept it opt-in
articles.text:
Someone inside Instagram proposed switching its break reminder on by default. The proposal was rejected because the cost to the app’s core metrics was not desirable.
George Volichenko, a former Meta data scientist, told that to a jury in Oakland this week. Mike Swift reported the testimony from the courtroom for MLex.
Volichenko worked on Instagram’s mental wellbeing team from April 2022 to February 2023. One of his first tasks was to measure how many teenagers used “Take a Break”, which prompts a 10-minute pause once a session passes a set length.
The answer was almost nobody
Roughly two in every 1,000 weekly teenage users took up the excessive-use features, Volichenko testified. He called that very low, almost negligible.
His team found fewer than 0.165% of teenage users switched the tool on and then took the break, Madlin Mekelburg reported for Bloomberg. A later review put it at 0.2%, which he called a drop in the ocean.
At the time, the tool required users to opt in. It was not part of the app’s default settings.
Why it stayed opt-in
Making it opt-out was considered and refused, on the grounds that the trade-off to core metrics was not desirable. In plain terms, Instagram expected to lose audience.
Volichenko described the internal reasoning to the jury. There was a lot of fear that an opt-out safety feature would produce large declines in those metrics, he said.
If that happened, he testified, multiple levels of leadership would have to report it upwards and explain why they were tanking the numbers.
The number Meta published instead
Adam Mosseri, the head of Instagram, wrote on Meta’s website in 2021 that early results were promising. Once teens set the reminders, more than 90% of them keep them on, he wrote.
Both things are true at once. Almost everyone who turned the tool on kept it, and almost nobody turned it on.
An allegation about how documents were marked
Volichenko also told the jury that it was standard practice at Instagram to put an attorney-client privilege label on essentially anything the company would not want the public to see.
That is sworn testimony from one former employee rather than a finding, and Meta has not responded to it publicly. Swift called it one of two significant moments in the evidence.
What his manager told him
He raised the low adoption figures internally. He was told not to worry, because the team existed partly to protect the company against the coming lawsuits.
His manager also told him to announce the findings as improvements to the tool, Carly Nairn reported for Courthouse News. Volichenko left in 2023.
Meta’s lawyer got something back
Brian Stekloff, cross-examining, put the same statistic the other way round. If you do the math, that is nonetheless hundreds of thousands of teens, he said. Volichenko agreed.
Stekloff established that the tool would not suit every teenager. Someone who opens the app many times a day, rather than scrolling in long stretches, may still be a problematic user and would never trigger a reminder.
Then he asked whether this had been a sham communication.
“No, it was accurate,” Volichenko replied. “Our goal was reached. I just did not think it was an ambitious enough goal.” Swift reported the exchange.
That answer matters. The states’ own witness declined to say Meta had lied about the tool, and objected instead to the size of the target it set itself.
He is there under subpoena
Volichenko is testifying under subpoena by the states and is not being paid for it, Swift reported. He has not appeared in any of the previous addictive-design trials where Meta was a defendant.
Meta has since changed the setting
This is the company’s strongest fact and nobody disputes it. Meta introduced teen accounts for under-18s, with Take a Break and other tools switched on by default, including one aimed at late-night use.
Anyone under 16 needs parental consent to turn those features off. In 2025, Meta said 97% of teenagers aged 13 to 15 keep the default restrictions on.
The states are not arguing about what the app does now. They are arguing about what Meta said while it did something else.
The default is the whole argument
Arturo Bejar is a former Meta engineer and was the states’ first witness. He told the jury last week that Take a Break was “designed to fail”.
It failed because most people never change that setting, Bejar said, and because the reminder could be snoozed away. He compared the design to having to switch on an airbag every time you get into a car.
What the case actually is
Chief US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers set out the scope from the bench. The trial is not about the content on the platforms, which Section 230 shields.
“The point of this trial is that Meta allegedly lied and misrepresented that the features are addictive,” she said. Had Meta said nothing, there would be no case.
Four states are bringing it: California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey. They say Meta breached the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act and made deceptive statements that misled the public.
The scale of it
An eight-person jury will give an advisory verdict, and Rogers decides the case and any penalties. Those could reach $200bn, Nairn reported, alongside orders changing how Meta runs teen accounts.
Meta has said the four states are seeking $1.4 trillion in penalties, a figure the company put on the record before the trial began.
This is the first case in litigation covering more than 3,000 active claims, and another 25 states go to trial later. Proceedings opened on 17 August and should run six to eight weeks.
Europe is settling this by rule instead
Oakland is arguing about whether a company can be liable for shipping a safety tool almost nobody found. Europe is answering the question before it reaches a courtroom.
The European Commission has charged TikTok with failing to protect children under the Digital Services Act. Australia has banned under-16s outright, and a watchdog says Meta has paid influencers to campaign against those bans.
What happens next
Volichenko finished on Tuesday. Giving up a large salary at Meta was probably the hardest thing he has ever done, he said, and the wellbeing team was not nearly as effective as it could have been with more agency and freedom.
Francesco Fogu, Instagram’s director of product design, took the stand next. Mosseri is also expected this week.
The case is People of the State of California v. Meta Platforms Inc., 23-cv-05448, in the Northern District of California.
